n: James warns that faith in the glorious Lord Jesus cannot go together with favoritism. Treating people differently based on status contradicts the Savior we follow.

f.g: Favoritism; judging people by outward rank or wealth.

n: He imagines a scene at church: a wealthy man walks in wearing gold rings and fine clothes, and a poor man arrives in dirty, shabby clothing.

f.g: Greek synagōgē — the gathering place or meeting of believers.

n: If the members rush to give the rich man the best seat while telling the poor man to stand or sit on the floor, something has gone badly wrong.

f.g: On the floor by my feet—a place of humiliation.

n: Such favoritism makes us biased judges with wrong motives, ranking people by appearance instead of seeing them as God does.
God has often chosen people the world calls poor to be rich in faith and heirs of His kingdom. The Lord’s values turn worldly rankings upside down.
James points out the irony: the members insulted the poor, yet it was the wealthy who were exploiting them and dragging them into court.

f.g: Courts of law, where creditors could press poor debtors.

n: These same powerful people mock the holy name of Christ by which believers are called. Why honor those who dishonor the Lord?

f.g: The name of Christ, taken upon believers.

n: The “royal law”—the King’s own law—is to love your neighbor as yourself. Living by it is exactly what God wants.

f.g: The supreme law, given by the King.

n: Playing favorites is not a minor social mistake; it is sin, and the law itself exposes it as breaking God’s commandment.

f.g: convinced = convicted, shown to be guilty.

n: God’s law is a unified whole. Breaking even one part still makes a person a lawbreaker—which is why everyone needs Christ’s mercy.
The same God gave all the commandments. Avoiding one sin while committing another still leaves a person guilty before Him.
Speak and act like people who know they will be judged by the law that frees us—the gospel of Christ.
The merciless will face judgment without mercy, but mercy wins out over judgment. Showing mercy invites God’s mercy toward us.
James begins his famous teaching: what good is claiming faith if it never shows in action? That kind of “faith” cannot save.

f.g: Literally ‘can that faith save him?’—meaning a faith with no works.

n: He gives an example: a fellow believer has no clothes and nothing to eat that day.

f.g: Often meant poorly or insufficiently clothed.

n: If someone just says “Go in peace, stay warm and well fed” and gives nothing, those kind words are useless. Real compassion acts.
Faith that produces no works is like a corpse—lifeless. True faith naturally shows itself in deeds.
James imagines a debate. Someone claims faith and works are separate gifts; James answers that you can’t show faith except through what you do.
Believing that God is one is good—but even demons believe that, and it only makes them shudder. Knowing facts about God is not the same as faith.

f.g: An echo of the Shema, Israel’s core confession.

n: James calls the objector an “empty” person and asks if he is willing to learn that faith without works is useless.
Abraham’s faith was proven when he obeyed God and offered Isaac on the altar. His belief showed itself in a costly act.
Abraham’s faith and his actions worked together, and his obedience brought his faith to full maturity.
His obedience fulfilled the scripture that Abraham believed God and was counted righteous. He even became known as the Friend of God.
James concludes that people are justified by faith that works, not by bare belief. Paul and James agree: real faith shows itself in obedience.
Rahab, a Canaanite woman in Jericho, also showed faith by action when she hid Israel’s spies and helped them escape.
James sums it up with a vivid image: a body without its spirit is dead, and so is faith without works.
